Residual Plots

Recall: Regression model residuals

The residuals for a model are

\[ y - \hat{y} \]

Residuals are used to:

  • Check a model: is the association really linear?
  • If the model is linear, measure how much variation in the response is explained by the model.

Residual plot: NBA Wingspan

The residual plot “detrends” the scatterplot

Residual Plots

Definition

Residual Plot: a scatterplot with

  • x-axis: explanatory variable
  • y-axis: residuals, \(y - \hat{y}\), from the model

What to look for:

  • no pattern (a null plot): indicates good model fit
  • curvature: then your model is not good!
  • It can also help to reveal outliers

Residuals: Forbes Experiment

Question

James D. Forbes 1857 experiment: Can atmospheric pressure be determined from the boiling point of water?

  • \(y\) = pressure
  • \(x\) = boiling point of water (temp)

Is the relationship linear?

Scatterplot:

Residuals: Forbes Experiment

Is the relationship between pressure and temp linear?

  • No. There is a curved relationship so a line should not be used to describe the relationship.
  • A line would
    • overestimate pressure for “middle” temps
    • underestimate pressure for low/high temps
  • Turns out that temp and log(pressure) have a linear relationship!

Residual Plots in R

  1. Fit linear model (using lm() function)
#linear model code
nba_lm <- lm(blk ~ wingspan_inches, data = nba)

Residual Plots in R

  2. Get residuals

broom package: augment() function adds residuals to a lm’s x/y variables

Residuals Plot with R Code

So? Is the relationship linear?

#Residual Plot
ggplot(nba_aug, aes(x = wingspan_inches, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(x = "Wingspan (inches)",
       y= "Residual (blocks per 100 possessions)",
       title= "Residual Plot: Wingspan vs Shot-Blocking")

R-squared

R-squared

Definition

R-squared measures the proportion (or percentage) of variability observed in the response \(y\) which can be explained by the explanatory variable \(x\).

\[R^2 = \text{explained variation} = 1 - \text{unexplained variation} = 1 - \frac{sd(resid)^2}{sd(y)^2} \]

  • Residuals give us information about what we weren’t about to explain
  • \(sd(y)^2\): variation in \(y\) (standard deviation of \(y\), squared)
  • \(sd(resid)^2\): variation from residuals, square of the standard deviation of the residuals
  • R-squared is the correlation coefficient squared in a simple linear regression model (one explanatory variable)

R-squared Interpretation

Interpretation

Regression of blocks per 100 possessions on wingspan for NBA players:

\[R^2 = 0.4354 \]

  • Wingspan explains about 43.5% of the observed variation in blocks per 100 possessions.
  • What factors (variables) besides wingspan might explain the other roughly 56.5% of variation in shot-blocking?

R-squared in R

R code

#linear model code
summary(nba_lm)

Digging Deeper in R-Squared

Can also calculate \(R^2\) using variation in R.

Using Variation

#variation in "y"
sd(nba$blk)^2
[1] 0.707828
#residual variation
sd(nba_aug$.resid)^2
[1] 0.3996392
#calculate R-squared:
1 - sd(nba_aug$.resid)^2/sd(nba$blk)^2
[1] 0.4354006

Adding a Categorical Variable

Adding a Categorical Variable

We should include confounding variables when possible/appropriate.

Two approaches (of many):

  • Augment scatterplot with colors for each category
  • Split (subset) data by categories, fit regressions for each group.

Example: Position as a Confounder?

Continuing our wingspan analysis:

  • Wingspan and blocks per 100 possessions
  • They are positively correlated!
  • But — bigs (centers/forwards) tend to have both longer wingspans and play closer to the rim (more blocks). Is position driving this relationship?
cor(nba$wingspan_inches, nba$blk)
[1] 0.6598489

Example: Position as a Confounder?

Plot the bivariate data

ggplot(nba, aes(x = wingspan_inches, y = blk)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)+
  labs(x = "Wingspan (inches)",
       y= "Blocks per 100 possessions",
       title= "Wingspan vs Shot-Blocking (NBA 2024-25)")+
  theme_minimal(base_size = 20)

Add Position (Confounder)

Let’s add a regression line for each group (Guard vs Big)

#add info on position group
ggplot(nba, aes(x = wingspan_inches, y = blk,
        col = position %in% c("C", "PF"))) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(color = "Big (C/PF)")+
  theme_minimal(base_size = 20)

What’s going on with Position?

  • Be careful when analyzing data that you are showing the full picture!
  • Confounding variable: a third variable (in addition to \(x\) and \(y\)) that affects both \(x\) and \(y\)
  • When you analyze the data while accounting for other variables, your findings might change
  • In this case, position matters a lot! Within Guards, wingspan barely predicts blocks (\(r \approx 0.17\)); within Bigs, the relationship is much stronger (\(r \approx 0.60\)).

Split and Redo: let’s check

Split the data

#split by position group
nba_guards <- filter(nba, position %in% c("PG", "SG"))
nba_bigs <- filter(nba, position %in% c("C", "PF"))

Recompute \(r\)

Guards:

cor(nba_guards$wingspan_inches, nba_guards$blk)
[1] 0.1708486

Bigs:

cor(nba_bigs$wingspan_inches, nba_bigs$blk)
[1] 0.6026932

(full data: \(r\) = 0.66)

Outliers

Outliers in Regression

Look for outliers that might affect the fitted model and correlation

  1. Fit the model/correlation with all cases
  1. Use which to help find potential outliers, following visual inspection
  1. Use slice or filter to create a data set without outliers OR, use subset within the lm command
  1. Fit the model/correlation without outliers to see the effects
  1. Report your findings from both analyses and data processing and interpret in context.

Rule of thumb: Pay attention when 1-3 points (or a small %) have a large influence on analysis

Outliers: Average SAT by State

How are average math and verbal SAT scores associated in midwest states?

Issue: Ohio and Indiana have SAT scores much lower than the other 10 midwest states.

Why might they be so different?

Outliers: Average SAT by State

Load in the lab manual dataset

sat <- read.csv("https://math.carleton.edu/Stat120/RLabManual/sat.csv")

Outliers: Average SAT by State

  1. Compute correlation/fit the model with all cases
  2. Exclude potential outliers
#find rows with low verbal score
which(sat_MW$verbal < 550)
## [1] 2 10

#filter these rows out
sat_MW_noout <- sat_MW %>% filter(!(verbal < 550))
sat_MW_noout

Outliers: Average SAT by State

  1. Compute correlation/fit the model with all cases
  2. Exclude potential outliers
  3. Fit the model/correlation without outliers
#correlation without outliers
cor(sat_MW_noout$math, sat_MW_noout$verbal)
## [1] 0.8465318

#fit linear model
sat_lm_noout <- lm( math ~ verbal, data=sat_MW_noout)
sat_lm_noout

## Call:
## lm(formula = math ~ verbal, data = sat_MW_noout)
##

## (Intercept) verbal
## 6.1453 0.9956

#calculate r-squared
summary(sat_lm_noout)$r.squared
## [1] 0.7166161

Outliers: Average SAT by State

  1. Compute correlation/fit the model with all cases
  2. Exclude potential outliers
  3. Fit the model/correlation without outliers
  4. Report your findings from both analyses
data r R-squared slope
all cases 0.973 94.7% 1.047
exclude IN/OH 0.847 71.7% 0.996
  • Without Indiana and Ohio: Correlation drops by 13%, slope by 5% and R-squared by 24%.
  • Conclusion: The strength of the association between math and verbal may be overstated when Ohio and Indiana are included.
